rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Cain and Abel account parallels Genesis and presents fallen humanity's tendency toward violence against its own brothers.
rows.anchor: like its Biblical version the Quranic story of Cain and Abel serves as a prototype of the inclination of fallen human beings toward violence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some commentators read the story in its sūrah context as a subtle commentary on issues concerning the People of the Book.
rows.anchor: the story is read by some commentators as offering a subtle commentary on issues related particularly to the People of the Book

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to recite truthfully may address Jews and/or idolaters who plotted to kill Muhammad and some Companions.
rows.anchor: Recite unto them, with truth may mean that Muhammad should relate this account to the Jews and/or the idolaters

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The idiom for stretching hands against someone links the plot against Muhammad in 5:11 with Cain's intent to kill Abel.
rows.anchor: The idiomatic phrase stretch forth their hands against is also used to describe the intent to kill in the present account

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The story may target Jews and Christians whose hostility to Muhammad's message arose from spiritual envy; envy among earlier religious communities is noted elsewhere.
rows.anchor: it may be directed at those Jews and Christians who were hostile to Muhammad’s message out of spiritual envy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account's conclusion with Israel's murder prohibition further suggests that the story was partly directed toward the People of the Book.
rows.anchor: further suggests that this account may have been directed, in part, toward the People of the Book

rows.speaker: al-Ṭabarī
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī says the story encourages Muslims to treat the Jews who plotted against Muhammad and his followers leniently, following Abel's restraint.
rows.anchor: Al-Ṭabarī, however, suggests that the reason for telling this story was to encourage the Muslims to deal leniently

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī cites a hadith telling Muslims to follow the better of Adam's two sons and leave the worse path.
rows.anchor: Verily God gives you the example of the two sons of Adam; so take [the path of] the better of the two

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adam's two sons are the Biblical Cain, Qābīl, and Abel, Hābīl.
rows.anchor: Adam’s two sons refers to the Biblical Cain (Qābīl) and Abel (Hābīl).

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: One account says God commanded the brothers to sacrifice; another says they competed for the right to marry Cain's twin sister, whom both desired.
rows.anchor: The two were either commanded by God to offer a sacrifice (Ṭ) or, according to some commentators, engaged in rival sacrifices

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Herdsman Abel offered a fattened sheep while crop-grower Cain offered produce.
rows.anchor: Abel, being a herdsman, offered a fattened sheep for the sacrifice, while Cain, who grew crops, offered some of his produce.

words: فَتُقُبِّلَ مِنْ أَحَدِهِمَا وَلَمْ يَتَقَبَّلْ مِنَ ٱلْءَاخَرِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an, like Genesis, identifies the accepted and rejected offerings but does not state why God chose one.
rows.anchor: but, like the Biblical account, does not indicate the reason for this choice.

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Some say Abel offered his prized sheep while Cain offered the poorest of his crops, explaining rejection of Cain's sacrifice.
rows.anchor: Some commentators explain that while Abel sacrificed his most prized sheep, Cain offered the poorest produce from his crop

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurbān derives from a root associated with nearness, so sacrifice is understood chiefly as a means of drawing near to God.
rows.anchor: Sacrifice here renders qurbān, a word whose root, q-r-b, is related primarily to nearness

rows.speaker: al-Ṭabarī
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī says both brothers primarily sought closeness to God, casting doubt on reports that their offerings competed for a woman.
rows.anchor: Al-Ṭabarī notes that closeness to God was the essential motivation of both Cain and Abel

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī attributes pious intent in the sacrifice only to Abel.
rows.anchor: al-Rāzī attributes pious intent in the sacrifice only to Abel.

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Abel implies Cain's offering was rejected because it lacked reverence or fear of God and was lowly and unfitting.
rows.anchor: the latter’s sacrifice was not accepted because it had not been done with proper “reverence” or fear of God

rows.speaker: al-Ṭabarī
rows.claim: For earlier communities sacrifice was analogous to Muslim charity; prayer, fasting, righteous acts, and obligatory alms take its place in Islam.
rows.anchor: Al-Ṭabarī notes that the practice of sacrificial offering for earlier religious communities was like the practices of charity and alms for Muslims

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb qarraba used for offering sacrifice can also describe giving charity.
rows.anchor: Offered a sacrifice translates qarraba, a verb that can also be used in connection with giving charity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because prayer, fasting, and charity parallel sacrifice, the verse broadly teaches that God accepts ritual and moral acts only when performed with reverence.
rows.anchor: only ritual or moral acts done with “reverence” are accepted by God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pilgrimage sacrifice and ʿĪd al-aḍḥā commemorate God's stopping Abraham's test and providing a ram; the meat is distributed as charity.
rows.anchor: both of which commemorate God’s halting Abraham’s test, during which he was to sacrifice his son

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The teaching that neither sacrificial flesh nor blood reaches God, but reverence does, partly supports al-Ṭabarī's charity analogy.
rows.anchor: Neither their flesh nor their blood will reach God, but the reverence from you reaches Him

words: مَآ أَنَا۠ بِبَاسِطٍۢ يَدِىَ إِلَيْكَ لِأَقْتُلَكَ
rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Commentators debate why Abel refused to oppose Cain or defend himself despite the explicit death threat.
rows.anchor: Commentators question why Abel refused to oppose his brother’s attack or defend himself

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Some say Abel's restraint clarified and emphasized the enormity of his brother's murderous intent and act.
rows.anchor: Some argue that this was a way of clarifying and emphasizing the enormity of his brother’s murderous intention and action

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Others say self-defense against an attacker had not yet been made lawful in early human history.
rows.anchor: attacking another in self-defense had not been made legitimate at this early stage of human history

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Others read Abel's words as rejecting preemptive intent or killing in self-defense, not necessarily all self-defense.
rows.anchor: is not necessarily an abandonment of self-defense, but an abandonment of the intention to kill his brother preemptively

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Some accounts say Cain killed Abel as he slept, leaving him unable to defend himself; this does not establish that he would not have fought while awake.
rows.anchor: Some accounts indicate that Cain killed Abel while he was sleeping, and Abel was thus unable to defend himself

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Another possibility is that Abel judged being killed preferable to killing, even in self-defense.
rows.anchor: Abel considered it better to be killed than to kill, even in self-defense

rows.speaker: al-Qurṭubī
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī says early pious Muslims, including ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar, cited Abel when abstaining from violence in the First Civil War; Abel showed strength by sparing a fellow monotheist, even a disobedient one.
rows.anchor: Al-Qurṭubī notes that the pious and prominent early Muslims who, like ʿAbd Allāḥ ibn ʿUmar, abstained from fighting fellow Muslims

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abel says he would rather let Cain bear the full burden of sin than attack his brother in return.
rows.anchor: rather than attacking his brother in return, Abel preferred to allow his brother to assume the full burden of the sin

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: My sin means the sin of killing Abel, not Cain bearing Abel's sins; the intervening word qatli is elided, since no one bears another's moral burden.
rows.anchor: none bears the moral burden of another—but rather that Cain would bear the burden of the sin of killing Abel

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Your sin refers to Cain's other acts of disobedience up to that time.
rows.anchor: your sin—that is, Cain’s sin—refers to the other acts of disobedience he had committed up to that time

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: The soul's prompting means it led or encouraged Cain, made murder easy, made it seem good, or emboldened him to commit it.
rows.anchor: it led or encouraged him to kill him, that it made it easy for him, or that it made it seem good to him and emboldened him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Soul can mean an individual moral entity or, in Qur'anic and pious/Sufi usage, the seat of passions driving wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: Although soul may simply refer to the individual as an independent moral entity, in certain verses in the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph's statement that the soul commands to evil illustrates the soul's role as a source of immoral impulses.
rows.anchor: Surely the soul commands to evil

rows.speaker: al-Qushayrī
rows.claim: Al-Qushayrī says once desire-driven soul has formed an evil intent, calls to right action become muted, perhaps explaining why Abel's words had no effect.
rows.anchor: al-Qushayrīremarks that once the soul—influenced as it is by its vain desires—has formulated an intention to do evil

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Most reports say Cain killed Abel in his sleep by crushing his head between two rocks; some say Satan taught Cain this method.
rows.anchor: According to most reports, Cain killed his brother in his sleep by crushing his head between two rocks

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: It is said Adam never laughed again after Abel's murder, although he lived many years afterward.
rows.anchor: Although Adam lived many years after Abel’s murder, it is said that he never laughed again

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Some commentators say Abel was the first human killed or even the first to die, explaining Cain's ignorance of corpse disposal and burial.
rows.anchor: Abel was the first person to have been killed, or even to have died, among human beings

rows.speaker: al-Ṭabarī
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī says burial had not yet been established; God sent a crow to bury another crow and demonstrate burial, teaching humans the rite.
rows.anchor: God then sent a living crow who “scratched the earth” with its beak and feet to bury another crow

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Other accounts say the crow dug to bury something else, inspiring Cain to bury Abel.
rows.anchor: the crow was digging in the earth in order to bury some other thing and this gave Cain the idea

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Another account says the crow covered Abel, and seeing the dignity given his victim made Cain remorseful.
rows.anchor: the crow came and began covering the dead Abel with earth, and when Cain saw how much dignity was afforded his victim

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sawʾah, rendered nakedness, can also allude to the private parts.
rows.anchor: Nakedness translates sawʾah, which can also be used to allude to one’s private parts.

rows.speaker: al-Zamakhsharī
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says sawʾah denotes the shame of Abel's exposed body, while al-Ṭabarī glosses it as corpse.
rows.anchor: Al-Zamakhsharī asserts that sawʾah here denotes the shame of Abel’s exposed body

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Waylatī is an exclamation of spiritual regret, often uttered when divine punishment becomes certain.
rows.anchor: Oh, woe unto me translates waylatī, which is an exclamation of spiritual regret

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The inability to conceal Abel's body and Genesis' image of his blood crying from the ground convey murder's horror and likely punishment in this world and the next.
rows.anchor: both suggest the particular difficulty of concealing a crime of murder

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Jewish Mishnah and Talmud likewise connect the life-equivalence principle to Cain and Abel, making it important in Jewish ethics.
rows.anchor: The Jewish commentary tradition as contained in both the Mishnah and the Talmud similarly connects this specific idea

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Some say killing a soul of exceptional spiritual importance, such as a prophet or just imam, is like killing all humanity.
rows.anchor: some commentators claim that the intended meaning is that killing a soul of particular spiritual importance

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Others understand the equivalence from the perspective of the person who was murdered.
rows.anchor: others say that killing a single soul is like killing all humanity from the point of view of the murdered individual

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Some consider murder grave as an offense against the Creator: killing one or many violates what God has made sacred.
rows.anchor: consider the gravity of murder from the perspective of its offense to the Creator

rows.speaker: Mujāhid
rows.claim: Mujāhid says afterlife punishment is equally grave for murderers regardless of victim count, since punishment for killing a believer does not increase with multiple victims.
rows.anchor: Mujāhid asserts that the punishment in the Hereafter is equally grave for all murderers

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Others read the equality as worldly punishment: a murderer can lose only one life whether he killed one victim or several.
rows.anchor: the worldly punishment for murder is the same for one or multiple victims

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception covers lawful execution for murder and other capital crimes, including adultery by married persons.
rows.anchor: The exception unless it be for another soul exempts killing in the course of carrying out lawful capital punishment

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Working corruption is understood as idolatry, warring against Muslims, or terrorizing roads; its penal consequences are discussed next.
rows.anchor: working corruption, understood to mean idolatry, warring against the Muslims, or terrorizing roads

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Saving a life can mean a victim's kin forgoing retaliation for compensation or forgiveness, or rescuing someone from fire or drowning.
rows.anchor: Whosoever saves the life of one is understood variously as referring to those who, as the kin of the murder victim

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Some broaden saving a life to indirect or spiritual help, including lifting someone from poverty or guiding the morally astray.
rows.anchor: Some broaden the idea of saving a life to include more indirect or spiritual modes of saving

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Some say Israelites are specified because they were the first community threatened with eternal punishment for murder.
rows.anchor: they were the first religious community threatened with eternal punishment for the sin of murder

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī says the Israelites are singled out because certain Jews of Medina allegedly plotted against the Prophet.
rows.anchor: al-Rāzī argues that the Children of Israel are singled out here because of the alleged plot of certain Jews of Madinah against the Prophet

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Other commentators say the moral principle applies equally to the Muslim community.
rows.anchor: Other commentators indicate that the moral principle applies equally to the Muslim community

rows.speaker: al-Ṭabarī
rows.claim: The verse continues the protector discussion from 5:51 and reiterates that believers should take only God, His Messenger, and believers as protectors.
rows.anchor: This verse continues the discussion of protectors begun in v. 51, reiterating that the believers should take only God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is the primary walī and Walī is one of His Names; taking the Prophet and believers as protectors follows naturally from one's relation of walāyah to God.
rows.anchor: one of whose Names is Walī, and one then takes His Prophet and the other believers as awliyāʾ

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Some see an endorsement of ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit, who left alliance with Jewish clans and pledged allegiance solely to the Prophet and his community.
rows.anchor: Some consider this verse to be an endorsement of ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Others read it as a response to Companions socially ostracized by Banū Qurayẓah and Banū Naḍīr.
rows.anchor: Others consider it to be a response to some Companions of the Prophet who complained about being socially ostracized

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Those praying and giving alms while bowing may refer to believers generally or sincere believers free from hypocrisy.
rows.anchor: can be understood as a description of the believers in general (Ṭ) or of the sincere believers who are untainted by hypocrisy

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Bowing while praying and giving alms may indicate performing these religious deeds humbly.
rows.anchor: may also indicate that one performs these religious deeds in a state of humility

rows.speaker: early authorities
rows.claim: Many early authorities, including Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid, specifically identify ʿAlī; reports describe him giving his ring to a person asking charity while he bowed in prayer.
rows.anchor: including the influential early commentators Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid, considered this to be a specific reference to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ʿAlī account encourages giving charity when requested and emulating his virtue in not delaying help until prayer ends.
rows.anchor: encouraging the practice of giving charity whenever it is requested and recommending that believers seek to emulate Alī’s high degree of virtue

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: A minority tradition identifies Abū Bakr as the referent.
rows.anchor: A minority tradition considers this verse to be a reference to Abū Bakr

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shiites call it the verse of wilāyah/walāyah; beyond protector or friend, these terms name a spiritual authority especially important in Shiism.
rows.anchor: Shiites sometimes refer to this verse as the “verse of wilāyah/walāyah.”

rows.speaker: Shiites
rows.claim: Shiites read the verse as identifying ʿAlī as walī after God and the Prophet, affirming his unique spiritual authority and right to succeed the Prophet.
rows.anchor: Shiites, who have used these terms traditionally to refer to the unique spiritual authority of ʿAlī

rows.speaker: Sunni authors
rows.claim: Some Sunni authors accept the early association with ʿAlī but say its traditions are unsound or do not establish Shiite legitimist conclusions.
rows.anchor: A number of Sunni authors who acknowledge the widespread connection of this verse to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī rejects spiritual authority as the meaning of wilāyah here, taking it as friendship or mutual support.
rows.anchor: Al-Rāzī, for example, denies that wilāyah/walāyah means anything other than friendship or mutual support here

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Despite Sunni objections to its legitimist reading, the widespread association with ʿAlī among Sunni commentaries and early authorities supports its authenticity in early tafsīr tradition.
rows.anchor: the prevalence of the association of this verse with ʿAlī, even in Sunni commentaries and among some of the earliest authorities

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those following 5:51 and 5:55 by taking God, the Messengers, and believers as protectors are called God's party; the term has been adopted by Islamic groups, including Hezbollah in Lebanon.
rows.anchor: Those who follow the injunction in vv. 51 and 55 to avoid taking protectors other than God, the Messengers, and the believers, are here described as the party of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's party in 58:22 consists of those who prosper and are content with God and whom God is pleased with; it is contrasted with Satan's party in 58:19.
rows.anchor: Party of God is also used in 58:22, where it is described as consisting of those who shall prosper
